CHARITABLE DEDUCTION CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Non-itemizer or itemized? Compare your 2026 charitable deduction.

Starting in 2026, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act gives non-itemizers a new above-the-line charitable deduction — up to $1,000 single, $2,000 married filing jointly. At the same time, itemizers face a new 0.5%-of-AGI floor that washes out the first slice of charitable giving on Schedule A. This tool runs both paths on your own numbers, side by side.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status

Single, head of household, and married filing separately all share the same $1,000 non-itemizer cap. Only married filing jointly gets the higher $2,000 figure.

2. Your numbers

Cash gifts to qualifying public charities only — not donor-advised funds, and not appreciated stock or property, which have their own separate limits this tool does not model.

Fill in your filing status, AGI, and cash giving, then click Calculate.

Comparison

Non-itemizer (above-the-line)

Itemized (after the new 0.5% floor)

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This compares one deduction under two paths — not total itemized deductions, whether itemizing beats the standard deduction overall, other credits, or state tax.
  • No top-bracket itemized-deduction limitation. OBBBA separately caps the tax value of ALL itemized deductions combined for the 37% bracket at 35 cents per dollar — flagged, not computed, since it needs your complete itemized total.
  • Cash gifts to public charities only. Donor-advised fund contributions do not qualify for the non-itemizer deduction at all, and appreciated property is separately limited to 30% of AGI — neither is modeled here.
  • No 60%-ceiling carryforward. Cash gifts above the 60%-of-AGI ceiling can sometimes be carried forward up to five years; this calculator does not model that carryforward.

Common questions

What is the new above-the-line charitable deduction for 2026?

Starting with the 2026 tax year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act lets a taxpayer who does NOT itemize claim a deduction for cash gifts to qualifying public charities directly against AGI — $1,000 for single, head-of-household, and married-filing-separately filers, $2,000 for married filing jointly. It works even while taking the standard deduction.

What is the new 0.5% AGI floor for itemizers?

Starting in 2026, if you itemize, your aggregate charitable contributions are deductible only to the extent they exceed 0.5% of your AGI. The first slice of giving up to that floor produces no itemized tax benefit at all — it is simply washed out, not carried forward.

Which path is better for me?

It depends on your AGI and how much you give. At low giving relative to AGI, the 0.5% floor can wash out most or all of an itemized deduction, so the fixed $1,000/$2,000 non-itemizer amount often wins. At high giving relative to AGI, the itemized path is usually larger since it has no fixed cap — only the 60%-of-AGI ceiling. This calculator compares the CHARITABLE component only; whether itemizing is worth it overall depends on your other itemized deductions too.

Does this work for a donor-advised fund contribution?

Not for the non-itemizer path — donor-advised fund contributions do not qualify for the new $1,000/$2,000 above-the-line deduction at all, only direct cash gifts to public charities do. This calculator assumes cash gifts to public charities throughout; it does not model donor-advised funds or gifts of appreciated property, which are separately limited to 30% of AGI.

Does this account for the new limit on itemized deductions for the top tax bracket?

No. OBBBA separately reduces the tax value of ALL itemized deductions combined for taxpayers in the top 37% bracket — a different computation that needs your complete itemized-deduction total, not just charitable giving. This calculator is scoped to charitable giving alone and flags that limitation as out of scope rather than modeling it.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal charitable-deduction rules to the numbers you enter. It does not know your other itemized deductions, verify your filing status, or model the top-bracket itemized-deduction limitation, and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

Planning several years of giving? The charity bunching planner searches every donor-advised-fund schedule for the largest tax saving.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Itemizing in a high-tax state too? See the SALT deduction cap calculator — another new 2025/2026 OBBBA itemized-deduction change, this one on state and local tax rather than charitable giving. Do you gamble? See the gambling loss deduction calculator — another new OBBBA itemized-deduction haircut, this one a 90%-of-winnings cap rather than a floor or ceiling.

Working this out by hand instead? See where a hand estimate of the two charitable-giving paths usually goes wrong.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. working out the 2026 charitable deduction by hand

The arithmetic looks simple — a fixed cap on one side, a percentage on the other. The part that goes wrong by hand is which rule applies to which path, and in what order.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
0.5% floor scopeApplies the new floor to the non-itemizer deduction too.Only reduces the itemized path — the non-itemizer above-the-line deduction is never touched by the floor.
Non-itemizer capTreats the $1,000/$2,000 cap as per-gift rather than per-year.Caps your TOTAL cash giving for the year at the filing-status figure, not each individual donation.
Order of limitsApplies the 0.5% floor to uncapped giving, before the 60%-of-AGI ceiling.Applies the 60%-of-AGI ceiling first, then subtracts the 0.5% floor from that capped figure.
Donor-advised fundsAssumes a DAF contribution qualifies for the non-itemizer deduction.Flags that only direct cash gifts to public charities qualify — DAF contributions do not.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Applying the new 0.5%-of-AGI floor to the non-itemizer deduction too. The floor only applies if you itemize on Schedule A — the new $1,000/$2,000 above-the-line deduction for non-itemizers is not reduced by it at all.

What's the second most common mistake?

Treating the $1,000/$2,000 non-itemizer cap as a per-gift limit rather than a total-for-the-year cap. It is the maximum deduction for ALL your cash giving to public charities combined in the year, not per donation.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Forgetting the order the limits apply in. The existing 60%-of-AGI ceiling caps what could ever be deductible first; the new 0.5%-of-AGI floor is then subtracted from that capped figure. Applying the floor to your full, uncapped giving figure overstates how much the ceiling costs you.

What eligibility mistake gets made most often?

Assuming a donor-advised fund contribution qualifies for the non-itemizer deduction. It does not — only direct cash gifts to public charities qualify for the new $1,000/$2,000 above-the-line deduction.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page knows your other itemized deductions, whether itemizing beats your standard deduction overall, or the separate top-bracket itemized-deduction limitation. Both apply the same published federal rules to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.
